title: Multimodal Bioelectroceutical Strategies for Alveolar Bone Regeneration in Diabetes and Aging
text:
Alveolar bone regeneration is critical for dental implant success, yet diabetic and aged
patients face poor outcomes due to chronic inﬂammation and impaired healing. This
project develops a multimodal bioelectroceutical therapy combining ionically conductive
scaffolds, small molecules, and electrical stimulation to restore bone regeneration. The
approach addresses inﬂammatory barriers and enhances osteogenesis, angiogenesis, and
neurogenesis, offering a transformative solution for compromised patient populations.

title: Biological and cancer-associated role of epitranscriptomic gene expression regulation
text:
Nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT) is a likely master regulator of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC)
gene expression through its hypomethylating effect on DNA, histones and mRNA; however, a link between
NNMT expression and mRNA hypomethylation has not previously been established as a mechanism
contributing to cancer progression. In my dissertation project, I am testing the hypothesis that NNMT activity in
TNBC cells results in 1) reduced m6A mRNA modification associated with altered protein expression of
pathways mediating cellular stress response and 2) cancer stem cell-like traits associated with survival,
metastatic potential and increased in vivo tumor-forming capacity. As accumulating research has been
highlighting the biological relevance of RNA modifications both in terms of normal physiology and pathology
including cancer, I plan to pursue my post-doctoral research on the biological and cancer-associated role of
epitranscriptomic gene expression regulation with a translational focus as an endpoint to develop novel
modulators of RNA modifications as potential cancer therapeutic agents.

title: Intersection of autophagy and vesicle trafficking in Her2-positive breast cancer
text:
Despite the remarkable progress in recent years, our knowledge about the mechanisms underlying breast
cancer metastasis, which are ultimately responsible for patient lethality, is still limited. The characterization of
molecular and cellular mechanisms at the intersection of key cellular processes, such as autophagy and vesicle
trafficking in HER2+ breast cancer cells, will significantly advance our fundamental knowledge about breast
cancer and contribute to novel therapies to eradicate this deadly disease.

title: Interrogating and Targeting Microglia Phagocytosis in Alzheimer’s Disease
text: The microglia surfaceome serves as a critical cellular hub that enables neuroprotective, neurotoxic, and neuroinflammatory signaling in the diseased brain. The ability to precisely target and manipulate diverse microglia states and function therefore holds tremendous experimental and therapeutic potential. The proposed project will use innovative tools and technologies to mechanistically interrogate and modulate microglia phagocytosis in Alzheimer’s disease and thus holds important therapeutic implications for treating this devastating disorder.

title: Genetics of Male Infertility: Accelerating the pace of discovery
text:
Program Narrative
Approximately 12% of men in the United States are subfertile or infertile. Infertility is a pervasive condition that
impacts not only the ability to have biological children, but has broader implications for psychological well-
being, relationships, finances (assisted reproduction and adoption can be expensive), overall health and life
expectancy. The objective of this NCTRI P50 Center for Reproductive Genetics and Therapy is to Improve
knowledge about the genetic basis of infertility to aid in the counseling of infertile couples; justify the
development of diagnostic screens; and develop patient-specific treatment options.

title: Novel Methods to Study Intra-Cortical Mu-Opioid Actions
text:
Frontal-cortical dysfunction is strongly implicated in numerous psychiatric disorders, including addictions and
eating disorders (EDs), which exact an enormous social cost and are very difficult to treat. Currently, only a
few, poorly effective medications exist for these disorders. A better understanding of frontal-cortical
neuromodulator systems could open entirely new avenues for drug development. An almost entirely
overlooked topic is the functional role of peptide-based neuromodulation in frontal cortex, despite
recent evidence that peptides (small amino-acid chains) produce unique effects relative to ‘classically studied’
cortical neuromodulator systems such as monoamines or glutamate. The goal of this project is to develop and
implement novel, cutting-edge techniques to (1) measure peptide release in frontal cortex, and (2) assess the
activity of the cells upon which cortical peptides act. These studies, the first of their kind, will enable us to
discover entirely new peptide systems and to better understand how peptides modulate cortical neurons. The
proposed work could identify new pharmacological targets to treat EDs and allied disorders.

title: Ultrasound-guided cancer immunotherapy with targeted nanodroplets
text:
There is a critical unmet clinical need for development of new, more effective immunotherapy strategies. Here
we propose to address this need by developing and evaluating an ultrasound-activated nanodroplet technology
that will enable innate-immunity-driven systemic activation of antitumor activity.

title: Defining Molecular Interactions Between Commensal Respiratory Viruses and the Human Host
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it focuses on developing and applying state-of-the-
art technologies to elucidate the role of commensal respiratory viruses and their interaction with the host,
including sequencing, proteomics, reverse genetics and primary cell models. These studies can help us
understand how commensal viruses replicate and persist in the host and influence host immunity, disease
susceptibility, and therapeutic response. Thus, the proposed research is relevant to the NIH’s mission that
pertains to “characterize the human virome and create tools, models and methods” to study its influence on
health and disease.

title: Human iPSC neural spheroids to screen for compounds that block tau propagation
text:
RESEARCH & RELATED Other Project Information
Novoron Bioscience, Inc.
8. PROJECT NARRATIVE
Tau protein, which is dysregulated Alzheimer’s disease, does not have any small molecule drugs to limit its
propagation. Organoids generated from LRP1 (low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein WT and KO
human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) provide a scaled-down and functional three-dimensional model
of the human brain, mimicking various developmental features at the cellular and molecular levels. We will use
this high-throughput screening compatible platform to test control and experimental drugs to address dementias
associated with tau propagation via LRP1, enabling a slowing and potential prevention of tauopathy hallmarks
in AD.

title: Oklahoma Center for Microbial Pathogenesis and Immunity
text:
Microbial infections and immunity have a dramatic impact on human health. The Oklahoma Center for Microbial
Pathogenesis and Immunity Phase 2 COBRE will support and train the next generation of academic
microbiologists and immunologists to advance basic research in infectious diseases and immunology. Through
this effort, we will grow the network of expert scientists and advance new discoveries that can be translated into
the next generation of vaccines and treatments.

title: Functional Characterization of LncRNAs Involved in Pluripotency or Differentiation
text:
We propose to determine the function of several prioritized long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) in pluripotency
and/or lineage commitment and identify the specific pathways that they regulate. In depth analysis will define
how these lncRNAs control differentiation processes through their impact on gene expression in cis or trans
and/or in other aspects of cellular function. The proposed studies will provide new insights as to how regulatory
signals instructed by lncRNAs can impact differentiation which will influence basic biology and disease states.

title: Epigenetic gene regulation for stem cell fates
text:
We are studying a key epigenetic mechanism controlling cell fates in stem cells. Components of this
mechanism are associated with pediatric cancers and developmental disorders, suggesting its crucial function
in human development. Our success will provide important insights on epigenetic regulation of human
embryogenesis and may advance our understanding of disease mechanisms.

title: PROTECTIVE POISON AT HIGH ALTITUDE: THERAPEUTIC EFFECTS OF ELEVATED ENDOGENOUS CO FROM ADAPTIVE HMOX2 VARIANTS
text:
Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a global health concern that is characterized by pulmonary arterial wall
thickening, vasoconstriction, and thrombus. Recent investigations of populations residing at high altitude
revealed that Tibetan highlanders are protected from pulmonary arterial hypertension, possibly through
adaptations in the heme catalysis and endogenous production of carbon monoxide. This project seeks to link
single nucleotide variants to observed adaptive phenotypes and translate them to further the understanding and
use of carbon monoxide releasing molecules in treating pulmonary arterial hypertension.

title: Developing strategies to identify candidate individuals for early genetic therapies
text:
The proposed work seeks to improve human health by developing strategies to risk stratify and identify
candidate individuals for genetic testing and treatment in early life. With therapeutic intervention becoming
available at earlier time points in life for treatable inherited genetic diseases, I aim to accelerate the time to
diagnosis for these conditions. Access to genomic diagnostics and therapeutics in early life is often limited; my
work aims to develop strategies to deliver genomic medicine and offer earlier opportunities for diagnosis and treatment.

title: Pathways Affecting Trophoblast Development
text:
(RELEVANCE STATEMENT)
Central to the etiology of disease processes leading to early pregnancy loss, preeclampsia, intrauterine
growth restriction, placentae abruptio, and pre-term birth is abnormal development of the uterine-placental
interface. Morphogenesis of the uterine-placental interface depends on differentiation and actions of the
invasive/extravillous trophoblast cell lineage. Elucidation of mechanisms controlling invasive/extravillous
trophoblast cell differentiation and its involvement in the development of the uterine-trophoblast cell interface
will lead to the discovery of diagnostics for early detection of failures in the establishment of pregnancy and
regulatory events that can be targeted for therapeutic intervention.

title: African Rare Diseases Initiative (ARDI): Advancing Genomic Medicine through rare diseases research in Africa
text:
About 1 in 20 individuals in the world could be affected by a rare disease. A good care starts with
a good diagnostics. Unfortunately, people from Low and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) do
not have access to good diagnostics. The situation of rare diseases in those countries is globally
unknown. Genomic medicine consists in using genomic information to make health decisions.
The fact that little is known from some parts of the world prevents those parts of the world from
having access to good genomic medicine. By helping rare diseases patients in the Democratic
Republic of Congo (DRC), we will also help patients in other regions of the world as well. The
DRC is a genomically rich country, where experienced clinical geneticists trained oversee are
now available and mobile internet has become available. We are a group of Congolese
researchers who have come together to build a network that will generate good quality
information and will improve the diagnosis in Congolese rare diseases patients, while also helping
non-African patients across the world. We will also develop a model and tools applicable to other
LMICs willing to embrace genomic medicine.

title: Medical Imaging Technology Development Core
text: ABSTRACT – Medical Imaging Technology Development Core The objective of the Medical Imaging Technology Development Core (MITDC) is to build an infrastructure to support research of the junior research project leaders (RPLs) and overarching goal of this COBRE. The Core will be built based on the OU Advanced Medical Imaging Center (OU-AMIC), which has been supported by both the Gallogly College of Engineering University of Oklahoma (OU) Norman campus and the Stephenson Cancer Center of OUHSC campus since 2012. OU-AIMC includes 5 research laboratories and an established network between the engineering and clinical expertise to facilitate the interdisciplinary research. OU-AIMC provides a solid foundation for this MITDC to provide important resource for RPLs and pilot project awardees of the COBRE. The MITDC Core has 3 Specific Aims. Aim 1: We will implement an interdisciplinary management plan to build an optimal infrastructure to support translational medical imaging related cancer research. The Core will be co- directed by an experienced engineer and a physician researcher. An advisory board of senior engineering and physician researchers will be established to guide the development and operation of the Core. Existing imaging equipment and other tools will be integrated to serve COBRE projects, along with equipment and services available by industry and clinical collaboration. Monthly brainstorming meetings, on demand tours, round table discussions, and biannual open house workshops will facilitate interaction between members of the Core and researchers on both OU Norman and OUHSC campuses. These activities will allow the Core to better understand researcher needs and provide opportunities for researchers to learn new imaging technologies that can benefit their research. Aim 2: We will design and develop a series of investigative imaging tools and testbeds to provide researchers fast and cost-effective methods to test their innovative research concepts. Using testbeds of new imaging modalities, the researchers will be able to acquire preliminary data to validate their hypotheses without the expensive and time-consuming development of a fully equipped laboratory. Based on the research areas of the initially selected RPL projects and other junior researchers in the COBRE pool, the testbeds will include, but are not limited to, phase-contrast X-ray imaging, X-ray fluorescence tomography, digital pathology scanners, and special optical imaging devices. Aim 3: We will build an integrated computer server/network and provide new computer-aided quantitative image feature analysis schemes and software to support the RPLs and other researchers to conduct large data and deep transfer learning-based Radiomics studies. This will improve the efficiency and consistency of developing and validating quantitative image markers and/or machine learning prediction models developed by different projects. In summary, MITDC will provide a unique research service and supporting capability to enhance the overarching goal of this COBRE. It will not merely be a collection of imaging equipment in a distinct space, it will also allow us to fully network our current research expertise to better support the translational cancer research using medical imaging technology to benefit patients in the future.

title: A Novel Shock-and-Kill with Shield Strategy Targeting HIV Latency and Neuroinflammation in CNS Reservoirs
text:
HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND) continue to affect more than half of people living with HIV,
despite effective antiretroviral therapy, in part because of persistent viral reservoirs and chronic brain
inflammation. This renewal project will build on our original R15-funded findings to extend the therapeutic
potential of combining FDA-approved cancer drugs, PARP and HDAC inhibitors, to both reduce latent HIV
reservoirs and protect brain cells from inflammation- and oxidative stress–induced damage. Successful
completion of this research could lead to new treatment strategies, termed "shock-and-kill with shield," to
improve long-term brain health and cognitive function in people living with HIV.

title: Transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation of human Treg identity and function
text:
Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are essential for maintaining immune homeostasis, but chronic inflammation can
cause Tregs to destabilize. Our recent CRISPR-based screens systematically identified key transcriptional and
post-transcriptional regulators of FOXP3, the lineage-defining factor required for Treg stability. Building on
these findings, we will use an integrated molecular and immunological approach to uncover mechanistic
insights into how multi-level regulatory networks control Treg stability, providing a comprehensive framework
for understanding the gene regulatory circuits governing Treg identity and function and ultimately informing the
rational design of next-generation Treg-based therapies with enhanced stability and efficacy.

title: Testing the efficacy of a new intervention for high intensity drinking among emerging adults
text: High intensity drinking (HID; episodes involving consumption of at least 8 standard drinks for women and 10 for men) among emerging adults (18-25 year-olds) places them at elevated risk for negative alcohol-related and mental health consequences, including development of alcohol use disorders and continued trajectories of high-risk alcohol consumption into adulthood. Experts have called for novel approaches tailored for people engaged in HID, a priority of NIAAA, and approaches that engage emerging adults can benefit from harnessing social media interactions given emerging adults’ high utilization of social media platforms. As a critical next step in addressing the public heath impact of HID, the proposed study will test the efficacy of an innovative social media-delivered intervention for HID that, when piloted, was found to be acceptable and feasible among emerging adults and demonstrated promise for improving alcohol use and mental health outcomes.
